<!-- Generated by `khora doc` from the `///` and `//!` comments in `std::core`. Edits here are overwritten; change the source. -->

The vocabulary every Khora program starts with.

`Option` and `Result`, the comparison and display traits, lists, arrays,
strings, vectors, maps and dictionaries, and the pieces structured
concurrency is built out of -- regions, fibers, nurseries and `Shared`.
Nothing here is optional in the way the rest of `std` is: two libraries
that disagree about what an `Option` is cannot exchange one.

## Where the effects went

Khora tracks effects as rows on the signature rather than as a wrapper
type, so there is no `Effect<A, R, E>` here. A computation's requirements
live in its `with` clause and its failures in its `raises` clause; both are
inferred on private functions and written out on exported ones.

The module is `std::core` rather than `std::effect` for two reasons: there
is no longer an `Effect` type to name it after, and `effect` is now a
reserved word, so `std::effect` will not lex as a path.

See docs/design/effects.md.

## Types

### Ordering

```khora
export type Ordering =
  | Less
  | Equal
  | Greater;
```

The result of comparing two values.

A three-way answer rather than two booleans: one comparison decides all six
operators, and a type cannot accidentally disagree with itself about `<` and
`>=`.

### Option

```khora
export type Option<A> =
  | Some(value: A)
  | None;
```

### Result

```khora
export type Result<A, E> =
  | Ok(value: A)
  | Err(error: E);
```

### List

```khora
export type List<A> =
  | Nil
  | Cons(head: A, tail: List<A>);
```

### Halves

```khora
export type Halves<A> = {
  left: List<A>,
  right: List<A>,
};
```

A list split down the middle, for `sort`.

### Step

```khora
export type Step<S, A> =
  | Yield(state: S, item: A)
  | Done;
```

One step of an iteration: the next item and the rest, or the end.

Khora has no mutable references and no mutable fields, so Rust's
`fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Item>` is not expressible. An iterator hands
back its successor instead. `for` desugars to this and reads the same.

### Range

```khora
export type Range = | Of(from: Int, to: Int);
```

`Range::Of(from, to)` yields `from` up to but not including `to`.

### Never

```khora
export type Never;
```

The empty type. A function whose return type is `Never` does not return
normally — it raises, diverges, or transfers control to a handler.

### Region

```khora
export type Region;
```

A region, and the finalizers deferred to it.

The type is here rather than hidden because `scoped` is written in Khora
and has to name it. Reference counted like everything else — which is the
whole mechanism: releasing the last reference runs the finalizers, and the
paths that release a binding are already the paths a region has to end on.

### Fiber

```khora
export type Fiber;
```

A running fiber, and the only way to wait for one or stop it.

Releasing a handle *joins*, so a fiber cannot outlive the binding that
holds it — on every path out, including a raise passing through. Put one in
a region and the region waits; put it in a block and the block does. That
is where structured concurrency comes from, and it needed nothing of its
own. `docs/design/fibers.md`.

### Array

```khora
export type Array<A>;
```

A fixed number of elements, side by side.

Fixed because growing is a *library* question and this is the primitive one
is built out of: `{ mut items: Array<A>, mut len: Int }` is a vector, and
it can be written in Khora now that a field can be written.

Reading an element is a bounds check and a load — no call — because the
layout is a contract with the code generator rather than something the
runtime hides. What the runtime does own is allocation and release, both of
which need the length at run time.

### Split

```khora
export type Split = {
  head: String,
  rest: String,
};
```

What `split_once` found: the text before the separator, and everything
after it.

### Ptr

```khora
export type Ptr;
```

An opaque machine address: a C `void *`.

**Not counted, not dereferenceable, and never a pointer into Khora's own
heap.** It exists so a foreign library can hand back a handle — a `FILE *`,
an `SSL_CTX *` — and be given it again later. Nothing in the language turns
a Khora value into one, which is what makes a dangling `Ptr` impossible:
every pointer that exists came from the other side, and its lifetime is
that side's business.

Lending a *buffer* across is the harder question and this type deliberately
does not answer it. `docs/design/ffi.md`.

### Chain

```khora
export type Chain<K, V> =
  | Empty
  | Node(key: K, value: V, rest: Chain<K, V>);
```

One bucket's worth of entries: the keys that hashed to the same slot.

Separate chaining rather than open addressing, because a chain is an
ordinary recursive ADT and needs no tombstones, no sentinel value and no
second array saying which slots are live. It allocates per entry, which is
the price, and it is the shape the language is actually good at.

### Pair

```khora
export type Pair<K, V> = {
  key: K,
  value: V,
};
```

A hash map from `Int` keys.

Written in Khora, out of an array for the buckets and a `mut` field for the
count — which is what phase 6 was for. Nothing below this is a compiler
feature.

Keys are `Int` because hashing a string means walking its bytes, and there
are no bytes yet — that arrives with fixed-width integers, and is the first
thing to revisit here.

The bucket count is always a power of two, which is what lets `slot` mask
instead of dividing. `new` starts at eight and `grow` doubles, so nothing
else has to maintain it.
One key and the value under it.

### Least

```khora
export type Least<K, V> = {
  key: K,
  value: V,
  rest: Dict<K, V>,
};
```

The smallest entry of a tree, and what is left without it.

### Dict

```khora
export type Dict<K, V> =
  | Empty
  | Node(size: Int, key: K, value: V, left: Dict<K, V>, right: Dict<K, V>);
```

An ordered map that is never written in place.

`Map` is the other one: a hash table that mutates its buckets, which is fast
and is exactly why it cannot cross a fiber or go in a `Shared`. This is
built out of ordinary variants, so it holds nothing writable and is
shareable in the ordinary structural way — a `Shared<Dict<K, V>>` is how a
cache several fibers use is spelled. `docs/design/shared.md`.

Persistent, so an insert gives back a new map and the old one is still
there. The two share everything the insert did not touch, which is what
makes that affordable: one path from the root is rebuilt, and the rest of
the tree is the same objects with one more reference each.

Weight-balanced (Adams), so every operation is logarithmic in the size and
the recursion here is bounded by the depth rather than by the length — the
distinction that `String::slice` got wrong and paid for.

### Map

```khora
export type Map<K, V> = {
  mut buckets: Array<Chain<K, V>>,
  mut count: Int,
};
```

### Vector

```khora
export type Vector<A> = {
  mut items: Array<A>,
  mut len: Int,
  mut wanted: Int,
};
```

A sequence that grows: an array, the part of it that is in use, and a
reallocation when those two meet.

The container to accumulate into. `Array<A>` is fixed at the length it was
allocated with, so a caller that does not know the count in advance cannot
use one; `List<A>` grows, but at the front, one allocation and one pointer
chase per element, and indexing it is a walk. This is contiguous, indexed
in constant time, appended to in amortised constant time, and — the point
of the whole exercise — *a constant number of allocations for any number of
elements*.

Fiber-local, like `Map` and for the same reason: the `mut` fields are what
make `push` cheap, and they are exactly what the sharing rules refuse to a
second fiber. A sequence several fibers write is a `Shared<List<A>>`, which
is slower and says so. `docs/design/sharing.md`.

**The obstacle, and what it cost to get around it wrongly.** `Array::new`
needs a value to fill with, and there is no value of an arbitrary `A` to be
had: `Vector::new()` has nothing in its hands, and neither has
`with_capacity`, whose whole purpose is to allocate *before* there is
anything to put in it. The first version of this type answered that by
holding `Array<Option<A>>` — every cell could then be `Option::None` — and
that answer was wrong in a way worth recording, because it type checked,
passed its tests and read perfectly well. It allocates a `Some` for every
element. A hundred integers pushed into a vector were a hundred and three
live objects, where they are two now, at that length and at every other:
the vector and its array. Allocating per element is precisely the property
a vector exists to *not* have, and it is the reason to reach for one over a
`List`. The other way out is a `new` that takes a seed element, which is
C++'s value-initialisation: it turns "give me somewhere to collect results"
into "produce a result first", and a type with no cheap value has to
fabricate one.

The answer is `Array::empty`, which is a zero-length array and needs no
fill because it has no cells. The storage starts there and costs nothing;
the first `push` allocates for real, and it can, because *the element being
pushed is the value to fill with*. Every cell of a fresh array holds that
element until a later push overwrites it, which for a boxed `A` is one
reference count per cell rather than one allocation per cell, and for an
`Int` is nothing at all.

`with_capacity` is the field that falls out of this: it cannot allocate
when it is called, so it records what was asked for in `wanted` and the
first `push` honours it. **A capacity is a promise here, not storage** —
`capacity` answers with what is really allocated, so a vector that has been
asked for a thousand cells and pushed to zero times still reports nought.
The alternative, reporting the promise, would be a number no memory
corresponds to.

What this costs against the `Option` cells is eager release. There is no
"empty" to write into a cell a `pop` vacated, so `pop` writes the vector's
first element there instead — a value of `A` it is guaranteed to have —
which releases the popped one just as promptly and costs a reference count.
Popping the last element and `clear` both drop the array outright, which
releases everything at once and is why neither keeps the storage; `wanted`
remembers the size, so refilling reallocates exactly once.

#### wanted

```khora
mut wanted: Int
```

How big the first allocation should be. Meaningless once there is one.

### SharedFn

```khora
export type SharedFn<A, B, 'e>;
```

The fibers a block is responsible for.

Releasing one *cancels its children and waits*, which is the answer for a
block that did not finish — a raise, or a cancellation, passing through. On
the ordinary path `nursery` has already waited, so the release finds
nothing to stop. That is how one value means both "wait for the children"
and "the answers are no longer wanted" without ever being told which
happened.
A function two fibers may hold.

A closure is never shareable on its own: what it captured is not in its
type, so no amount of looking at `(Request) -> Response` says whether the
thing behind it can be written. That is fine until a container of closures
has to cross — a router holding its handlers, a table of callbacks — at
which point the whole container is stuck on this side.

This is the proof, reified. `SharedFn::of` accepts only a closure written at
the call, where the captures are on the screen and can be checked; what it
returns has forgotten how it was made, and is shareable because the check
already happened. A `Route` holding one is shareable in the ordinary
structural way, with nothing special said about routers.

The cost is the wrapper at the mount site, and that is the honest price: the
alternative is a bit in every function type, which colours every container
of a function all the way up. `docs/design/sharing.md`.

### Changed

```khora
export type Changed<A, B> = {
  state: A,
  result: B,
};
```

A value two fibers may both change.

The sharing rules refuse a mutable record to a second fiber on purpose, and
refuse a handler that captures one, because two fibers writing one value is
a race. This is what they refuse them *until*: a cell holding a value, with
the reads and writes serialized.

**Mutation becomes replacement.** There is no borrow of the inside — a
counter is `Shared::update(count, fn n => n + 1)`, not `count.n = count.n + 1`
— and that is the whole of why this is safe rather than careful. Handing out
the inner value would mean stopping it escaping the critical section, and
without lifetimes there is no way to say that. Nothing unshareable goes in
or comes out, so there is nothing to leak. `docs/design/shared.md`.

The contents must be `Share` for the same reason, which also means a `Map`
cannot go in one: it mutates its buckets in place. `Dict` is the ordered
persistent map, and is what a shared table is made of.
A new state, and something to hand back that is not the state.

What `Shared::modify` asks its change function for. A record rather than a
tuple because a tuple literal has no expression form yet, and named halves
read better than positional ones at the call anyway.

### Channel

```khora
export type Channel<A>;
```

A bounded queue one fiber puts values into and another takes them out of.

**`Shared<A>` is a cell; this is a hand-off.** The two answer different
questions and the difference is what a value *is* while it is in flight. A
cell holds one value that anybody may read or replace. A channel holds a
queue of values that each go to exactly one taker, and — the part that
matters — a fiber waiting at either end **gives its worker back** rather
than spinning or blocking a thread.

#### What it is for

Three things, and they are the same thing seen from different sides.

**Owning a resource that cannot be shared.** A handler may not capture
anything writable, and a database connection is writable *and* strictly
serial — two fibers writing one socket interleave their frames. So one
fiber owns the connection and the others send it requests. The handler
captures the channel, which is `Share`, and never the connection, which is
not. This is why the type exists: `packages/postgres` could not be finished
without it.

**Backpressure.** A full channel stops the sender until a taker catches up.
That is not a limitation to be worked around; it is how a service under
more load than it can serve declines work at the edge instead of queueing
it until memory runs out.

**A pool.** A channel holding the four idle workers *is* the pool: taking
one is a receive, giving it back is a send, and waiting for one is what the
channel already does.

#### Closing

`close` says nothing more will be sent and releases everybody waiting. A
receive then drains what is already queued **before** answering `None`,
because values already sent are still worth having. Closing twice is
allowed: the fiber that owns a channel and the fiber that finishes with it
are often different code, and neither should have to know which went first.

#### What it does not do

**No rendezvous.** `bounded(0)` gets a capacity of one rather than a
channel where a send waits for a receive. Zero is a useful thing and it is
not this thing; building it here would mean a sender waiting on a receiver
that is waiting on a sender, and getting that wrong is a hang rather than
an error.

**No select.** Waiting on the first of several channels wants a primitive
of its own, and nothing has needed one yet.

### Schedule

```khora
export type Schedule = {
  attempts: Int,
};
```

How many times to run something, and when to stop.

Deliberately a plain description rather than a stream of instants: a
schedule with no clock in it can be read, compared and tested, and the
clock arrives later without changing what a policy *means*.

#### attempts

```khora
attempts: Int
```

Attempts in total, including the first. `1` is "do not retry".



### Ord

```khora
export trait Ord: Eq
```

Ordering refines equality: anything orderable can be compared for equality,
so `Ord` requires `Eq` rather than repeating it.

#### cmp

```khora
fn cmp(self, other: Self) -> Ordering
```

### Hash

```khora
export trait Hash: Eq
```

A value that can be a key.

Requires `Eq` rather than repeating it, because the two have to agree: a
map finds a key by hashing it to a bucket and then comparing, so **equal
values must hash equal**. Unequal values may collide — that is what the
bucket's chain is for — but two values that `eq` says are the same and
`hash` sends to different buckets are an entry that can be inserted and
never found.

`Float` is deliberately not an instance, because it is not an instance of
`Eq`: `NaN == NaN` is false, and a key that is not equal to itself is a
lost entry in every language that allows one. `docs/design/numbers.md`.

#### hash

```khora
fn hash(self) -> Int
```

A number to bucket by. Any number: spreading it out is the map's job, not
this one's, so an implementation only has to be *consistent*.

### Show

```khora
export trait Show
```

#### show

```khora
fn show(self) -> String
```

### Share

```khora
export trait Share
```

Two fibers may hold this at once.

A marker: no methods, and implementing it asserts rather than provides.
Nothing has to write it for an ordinary type — a record, a variant, a tuple
is shareable exactly when everything inside it is, and the compiler can see
that. This is for the types it *cannot* see inside: one declared with no
body, whose behaviour lives in the runtime or across the C ABI.

Those default to unshareable, which is the only safe way round. `Array` can
be written through `Array::set` and `Ptr` points at memory this language
did not allocate; both look like empty structures and neither is safe for
two fibers to share. So the author says which is which, and the reader can
see where the assertion was made.

Fibers are operating-system threads today, so this is `Sync` rather than
`Send`: both fibers keep their reference, and neither hands it over.

`docs/design/sharing.md`.

## Effects

### Scope

```khora
export effect Scope {
  defer: (() -> ()) -> (),
}
```

Resource lifetimes.

A finalizer registered with a scope runs when the enclosing region ends,
however it ends: falling off the end, an early `return`, or a raise passing
through.

The operation takes only a thunk. A handler's fields are ordinary closures
and a closure is monomorphic, so an operation cannot be generic — and it
need not be: `acquire` below is an ordinary generic function that closes
over the value and the release, which is where the polymorphism belongs.

### Nursery

```khora
export effect Nursery {
  adopt: (Fiber) -> (),
}
```

Where a spawned fiber goes.

The operation takes a fiber rather than a thunk for two reasons. A handler's
fields are closures and a closure cannot be generic, so an operation could
not be generic in what the thunk raises. And a thunk cannot be *forwarded*
to `Fiber::spawn` at all: a fiber's body has to be written where it starts,
so that what it closes over can be checked against the rule that a mutable
value may not cross. `docs/design/memory.md` §5a.

So the idiom is one call inside another, and the body is on the screen:

```
nursery.adopt(Fiber::spawn(fn () => analyze(id)!));
```

### List<A>

```khora
impl<A: Ord> List<A>
```

#### sort

```khora
fn sort(self) -> List<A>
```

The same elements, in order.

A merge sort, because a linked list is what it was invented for: it needs
no indexing, no copying into an array and back, and it is stable — equal
elements keep the order they were given, which is the property a caller
notices the absence of when sorting by one field and expecting the
previous sort to survive.

`A: Ord` rather than a comparison function, so that `<` on the elements
and `sort` on the list cannot disagree. Sorting by something else is
`sort_by`, which does not exist yet and wants a closure.

#### split

```khora
fn split(self) -> Halves<A>
```

The first half and the second, each in the order it was given.

**By counting to the middle, not by dealing alternately.** Dealing is one
pass and needs no length, and it is what this did first — but it is not
stable, and the test said so. Two equal elements at positions 1 and 2 land
in *different* halves with the later one on the left, and a merge that
breaks its tie towards the left then puts them back the wrong way round.

The cost is a length and a reversal, both linear, against a sort that is
already linearithmic.

#### take_first

```khora
fn take_first(self, count: Int, taken: List<A>) -> Halves<A>
```

#### merge

```khora
fn merge(self, other: List<A>) -> List<A>
```

Two sorted lists, as one.

`<=` rather than `<` on the tie, which is exactly what makes the sort
stable: an element from the left half goes first when they are equal, and
the left half is the earlier one.

#### spawn

```khora
fn spawn<'e>(body: () ->() raises 'e) -> Fiber
```

Runs `body` on a fiber of its own.

The thunk may fail, and a thunk that can is also one that can be
*stopped*: a cancellation travels out on the same tagged return an error
does, so a fiber with no error row has no channel to be interrupted on
and runs to its end.


Waits for the fiber to finish. Joining twice is joining once.

#### cancel


### Array<A>

```khora
impl<A> Array<A>
```

#### empty

```khora
fn empty() -> Array<A>
```

No elements at all.

`new` needs a value to fill with and a generic container has none to give
until something has been put in it, so without this there is no way to
write down an empty `Array<A>` — `Array::new(0, fill)` still demands the
`fill` it will never write. That gap is what `Vector<A>` is built on: its
storage starts here and is allocated for real by the first `push`, which
is also the first moment there is a value of `A` to fill with.

#### new

```khora
fn new(length: Int, fill: A) -> Array<A>
```


#### get

```khora
fn get(self, index: Int) -> A
```

The element at `index`.

An index outside the array stops the program and says which index and
what length. Same reasoning as trapping on integer overflow: a program
that runs off its own array is wrong, and reading whatever is next in
memory is the least useful possible response.


#### is_utf8

```khora
fn is_utf8(self) -> Bool
```

Whether these bytes are well-formed UTF-8, and so whether
`String::from_bytes` will accept them. Only an `Array<U8>` has an answer.

#### prefix

```khora
fn prefix(self, count: Int) -> Array<A>
```

The first `count` elements, copied.

What a caller does with a buffer it only partly filled: a socket read
says how many bytes arrived, and the rest of the buffer is not part of
the message.

#### with_data

```khora
fn with_data<B, 'c, 'e>(self, body: (Ptr, Int) -> B with 'c raises 'e) -> B with 'c raises 'e
```

Lends the elements to `body` as a pointer and a count, for the duration
of the call and no longer.

This is how a buffer reaches a foreign function. The count is the number
of *elements* — the same number `length` gives — so a body that wants
bytes multiplies by the element's width itself.

**The lifetime is the call, and that is the design rather than a
limitation.** A plain `data(self) -> Ptr` would be a dangling pointer
waiting to happen: the array is released at its last use, and that use
would be the `data` call. No wider scope is right either — the innermost
one is wrong for a pointer taken in one branch of an `if`, and the
function's own is wrong for a loop, which would hold one buffer alive per
iteration.

Only an array of numbers can be lent. An `Array<A>` of Khora objects
holds reference-counted pointers, and handing those across is the mistake
the whole boundary exists to prevent. `docs/design/ffi.md`.

asks for it at every step.

#### is_empty


```khora

```

A node whose size is computed from its children, and no balancing.

What the rotations build with: they already know the shape is sound, and
asking `balance` again would recurse.

#### balance

```khora

```

Rebuilds a node, rotating if one side has outgrown the other.

A side may be at most three times the weight of the other. Three rather
than two because two is not enough slack to keep a single insert from
rotating on every level, and much more than three stops bounding the
depth usefully.

#### rotate_left


single one moves its left subtree across, which only helps if that
subtree is the lighter half.



Every entry, smallest key first.

#### gather


The right side first, so what comes out is in key order.

An accumulator rather than two lists joined, so nothing is walked twice
and the recursion is the tree's depth.

Joins two sides whose node has gone.

The successor moves up: every key on the left is smaller than every key
on the right, so the smallest of the right is the one that can sit
between them.

### Map<K, V>

```khora
impl<K: Hash, V> Map<K, V>
```

#### new

```khora
fn new() -> Map<K, V>
```

An empty map, which allocates nothing but itself.

**The buckets wait for the first insert.** An empty map used to cost an
eight-element array, and a great many maps are never written to: a
request with no query string still builds a query map, a route with no
`:name` still builds one for its parameters, and both were paid for on
every request a server answered. `Array::empty` is what makes the
difference, and it did not exist when this was written.

#### len

```khora
fn len(self) -> Int
```

#### get

```khora
fn get(self, key: K) -> Option<V>
```

#### holds

```khora
fn holds(self, key: K) -> Bool
```

#### insert

```khora
fn insert(self, key: K, value: V) ->()
```

Adds `key`, replacing whatever was there. The count only moves when the
key is new, which is what makes it the number of entries rather than the
number of insertions.

#### remove

```khora
fn remove(self, key: K) ->()
```

#### entries

```khora
fn entries(self) -> List<Pair<K, V>>
```

Every entry, as a list.

**In no particular order.** A hash table forgets the order its keys
arrived in, and the order this does report is not even stable across
inserts: growing rehashes everything into twice as many buckets and moves
roughly half of it. A caller that wants an order sorts what comes back,
or uses `Dict`, whose `entries` is in key order because the tree already
is.

Without this, iterating a map means reaching into `buckets` and matching
on `Chain`, which is what `std::json` had to do to write an object back
out — a module coupled to the table's representation for want of six
lines here.

Two loops rather than two recursions. A table with a million entries has
a million buckets to visit, and a stack frame each is the mistake
`String::slice` made per byte. The inner walk is a loop too, for a less
obvious reason: a chain is only short while the `Hash` is good, and a bad
one puts every entry in a single bucket. The price of that should be a
slow walk, not a smashed stack.

#### keys

```khora
fn keys(self) -> List<K>
```

The keys, in the reverse of the order `entries` reports them — which is
to say in no particular order either.

Built by walking `entries` rather than the buckets a second time. The
pairs it allocates and throws away are the price of having one place
where the traversal is written; a map big enough for that to matter wants
`entries` itself, which allocates the pairs the caller was going to keep.

Not `List::map`, which recurses once per element and would put a ceiling
on the size of map this can be called on.

`keys` and `values` walk the same list the same way, so the two line up
position for position. That is the only thing worth promising about the
order of either.

#### values

```khora
fn values(self) -> List<V>
```

The values, one per entry — duplicates included, because two keys may
well hold the same value and dropping one would make `values` disagree
with `len`.

#### slot

```khora
fn slot(self, key: K) -> Int
```

Which bucket a key belongs in.

Knuth's multiplicative constant, then a shift-xor so that the high bits —
where multiplication puts the information — reach the low ones the mask
keeps. Wrapping on purpose: overflow is where the mixing comes from.
Which bucket a key belongs in.

Negative when there are no buckets, which is the empty map: every reader
checks for it, because masking against a length of zero would ask for
element -1.

#### grow

```khora
fn grow(self) ->()
```

Twice the buckets, and every entry moved into the new ones.

#### rehash

```khora
fn rehash(self, chain: Chain<K, V>) ->()
```

### Vector<A>

```khora
impl<A> Vector<A>
```

#### new

```khora
fn new() -> Vector<A>
```

Empty, holding no storage at all.

Eight is what the first `push` will ask for, matching `Map::new`'s eight
buckets — enough that a small vector never reallocates, small enough that
a vector which is made and never pushed to, as a field on a record or an
accumulator on the branch that turned out to have nothing to accumulate,
has cost two objects and no cells: itself, and the empty array's header.

#### with_capacity

```khora
fn with_capacity(capacity: Int) -> Vector<A>
```

Room for `capacity` elements, from the first `push` onwards.

Nothing is allocated here — there is no value of `A` to fill an array
with yet — so this records the size and the first `push` allocates it.
The saving is real either way: what `with_capacity` buys is that filling
it reallocates once instead of a dozen times, and that is a property of
the first allocation's size, not of when it happens.

A capacity that is not positive is no opinion at all, and gets the same
eight `new` would have. `Array::new` would trap on a negative length, and
rightly, but a capacity is a hint about a size that is often computed —
`expected - already_have` — and being wrong about a hint is not the same
kind of mistake as indexing off the end of an array.

#### length

```khora
fn length(self) -> Int
```

How many elements are in it.

#### is_empty

```khora
fn is_empty(self) -> Bool
```

#### capacity

```khora
fn capacity(self) -> Int
```

How many elements fit before the next reallocation — allocated cells, not
promised ones, so this is nought until the first `push`.

Worth exposing because growth is the only thing about a vector that is
not visible from the outside, and a test that means to exercise it has to
be able to see it.

#### push

```khora
fn push(self, item: A) ->()
```

Adds an element at the end.

The element goes to `grow` as well when the array is full, because it is
the fill: the only value of `A` anyone here has.

#### grow

```khora
fn grow(self, seed: A) ->()
```

Twice the room, or `wanted` if there was none, with `seed` in every cell.

**Doubling, not a fixed increment**, which is the whole reason `push` is
amortised constant: growing by a constant makes filling a vector
quadratic in its length, and that is the bug that turns a working program
into a slow one only once the input gets big. Two rather than the 1.5
some allocators are tuned for, because reusing the freed blocks needs an
allocator that coalesces them and this runtime hands them straight to
`malloc`; the smaller factor would buy nothing and copy more often.

The cells past `len` hold `seed` — a copy of the element being pushed,
because there is nothing else of type `A` to put there. They are
overwritten by the pushes that follow, and until then a boxed `A` is held
by that many references rather than that many objects.

The one visible consequence: a vector that grew and was then popped back
down keeps that element alive, because the cells above the length were
never written over. It is a single object however long the vector is —
all of those cells hold the same one — and it goes at the next growth or
with the array. Blanking them would need a value of `A` to blank them
*with*, which is the same wall this whole type is built around.

#### pop

```khora
fn pop(self) -> Option<A>
```

Removes the last element and hands it back.

`Option::None` from an empty vector rather than a trap: draining one is
`match Vector::pop(v)` until it answers `None`, which makes empty a loop
condition rather than a mistake. That is the opposite call from
`Array::get`, and deliberately — an index is a claim about a length the
caller believes it knows, while popping is a question.

The cell that is left over has to hold *something* of type `A`, so it is
given the first element. That is not tidiness: without it the array would
go on holding the element that was just removed, and a vector popped down
and then kept would be indistinguishable from a leak. Popping the last
element has no first element to use and needs none — the array goes, all
at once, and `wanted` keeps its size for the next fill.

#### get

```khora
fn get(self, index: Int) -> Option<A>
```

The element at `index`, or `Option::None` if there is none there.

Soft where `Array::get` traps, and not only for symmetry with `pop`: an
array's length is fixed and known where it was allocated, while a
vector's is whatever the pushes left it at, so a caller reading one is
far more often asking than asserting.

Bounded by `len` and never by `Array::length`. The cells in between are
not empty — they hold the fill, or an element a `pop` left behind — and
handing one of those back would be a phantom element rather than an
error.

#### set

```khora
fn set(self, index: Int, value: A) -> Bool
```

Replaces the element at `index`. Answers whether there was one to
replace.

A write past the end is not a question with an answer — there is no
element there — so this reports rather than inventing one or growing to
fit. Growing would have to fill the gap between, and the gap is exactly
what there is no value of `A` for; `push` is how a vector gets longer.

#### clear

```khora
fn clear(self) ->()
```

Empties it.

The array goes rather than being kept and blanked, because there is
nothing to blank a cell *with*: keeping it would keep every element in it
alive until something was pushed over that cell, and a cleared vector
holding its contents is the bug this method is usually called to avoid.
`wanted` remembers how big it was, so the next fill reallocates once and
arrives back where it started.

#### to_list

```khora
fn to_list(self) -> List<A>
```

The elements, first to last.

Backwards through the array, prepending, so the list comes out in order
without a reversing pass — the same trick `Map::entries` uses, and a loop
for the same reason: one frame per element is what `String::slice`
overflowed the stack with.

#### from_list

```khora
fn from_list(items: List<A>) -> Vector<A>
```

A vector of the list's elements, in the same order.

Pushed one at a time into an empty vector rather than sized up front with
`List::length`: that walk recurses once per element, so a list long
enough to be worth pre-sizing for is a list long enough to overflow the
stack being measured. Doubling costs a handful of reallocations and no
stack at all.

### Shared<A>

```khora
impl<A: Share> Shared<A>
```

#### of

```khora
fn of(value: A) -> Shared<A>
```

A cell holding `value`.

#### get

```khora
fn get(self) -> A
```

What is in it now, as a value of the caller's own.

#### set

```khora
fn set(self, value: A) ->()
```

Replaces what is in it.

#### update

```khora
fn update(self, change: (A) -> A) -> A
```

Reads, transforms and writes as one step, and gives back the new value.

`change` runs once, under the lock. It cannot fail, and that is
deliberate: a function with no error row has no channel to be cancelled
on, so nothing can leave the critical section except by returning and
there is no path on which the lock is still held. Work that can fail
belongs outside — compute it, then `set` the answer.

Updating the same cell from inside `change` is a deadlock, and stops the
program with a message rather than waiting for itself.

#### modify

```khora
fn modify<B>(self, change: (A) -> Changed<A, B>) -> B
```

The same, for a change that has something to say beyond the new state.

`update` can only answer with what it left in the cell, which is not
always what the caller needs to know. A handler inserting a record under a
generated key has to get *that* key back, and searching the new state for
it afterwards is a guess — a wrong one the moment two fibers insert
records that look alike:

```khora
let code = Shared::modify(links, fn table => {
  let drawn = fresh_code(table);
  { state: Dict::insert(table, drawn, made), result: drawn }
});
```

Both halves are installed and handed back under the one lock, so the
answer belongs to the state it was produced with.

### Fibers

```khora
impl Fibers
```

#### open

```khora
fn open() -> Fibers
```

#### bounded

```khora
fn bounded(limit: Int) -> Fibers
```

A nursery that will hold at most `limit` running children.

Adopting past the limit waits for the oldest to finish. That is the whole
of it, and it is what turns a capacity ceiling into a queue: a server
adopting a fiber per connection meets an unbounded nursery's ceiling by
exhausting memory, and meets a bounded one's by accepting more slowly,
which the listening socket's backlog is already built to absorb.

Unbounded is right for a nursery over a known handful of tasks — the
shape `nursery(..)` is usually used for — and wrong for one fed by the
outside world.


#### wait

```khora
fn wait(self) ->()
```

Waits for every child, oldest first, and empties the nursery.

## Functions

### assert

```khora
export fn assert(condition: Bool)
```

Fails the test this is written in, if `condition` is false.

Only allowed inside a `test` block, and inside one it needs no `!`. Both
halves of that are deliberate: an assertion is the one place a reader of a
test already expects control to leave, it is written at every one of them,
and a test is not ordinary code. `docs/design/testing.md`.

### print

```khora
export fn print(value: String)
```

Writes a line to standard output.

Declared without a body, so it is an extern: the backend dispatches it on
the argument's type, because there is no prelude yet to declare three
differently-typed printers. It is not an effect, which it eventually should
be — writing to a console is exactly the sort of thing a capability is for.

### nursery

```khora
export fn nursery<A, 'e, 'r>(body: () -> A with { 'e | nursery: Nursery } raises 'r) -> A with 'e raises 'r
```

Runs `body` with a nursery, and does not return until its children are done.

Structured concurrency, and the structure is the region's: a fiber cannot
outlive this block, because leaving it — at the end, on a `return`, or with
a raise passing through — releases the nursery, and releasing a nursery
stops what is still running.

**Pass a named function, not a lambda.** A named function receives what its
`with` clause names as evidence parameters, so it can be handed here and
called with the nursery this function installs:

```khora
fn serve<'e>() -> () with { 'e | nursery: Nursery } { .. }
nursery(serve)!
```

A lambda cannot, and `nursery(fn () => serve()!)` is refused: a lambda's
requirement row is always empty, because it *captures* the capabilities it
uses rather than receiving them — and this thunk was written before the
binding existed, so there is nothing to capture.

Which makes eta-expansion change meaning, and it should not.
`docs/design/capability-passing.md` decides what to do about that.

### bounded_nursery

```khora
export fn bounded_nursery<A, 'e, 'r>(limit: Int, body: () -> A with { 'e | nursery: Nursery } raises 'r) -> A with 'e raises 'r
```

The same, holding at most `limit` children at once.

**Which one to reach for is a question about where the work comes from.**
A nursery over a known handful of tasks — three lookups in parallel, a
fan-out over a list you are holding — should be unbounded, because the
count is already bounded by the thing you are iterating. A nursery fed by
the *outside world* should not be, because then the count is somebody
else's decision.

A fiber is an operating-system thread today, so unbounded there means a
ceiling met by exhausting memory. Bounded means one met by adopting more
slowly, which for a server means accepting more slowly, which the listening
socket's backlog is already built to absorb: overload becomes latency
instead of collapse.

### scoped

```khora
export fn scoped<A, 'e, 'r>(body: () -> A with { 'e | scope: Scope } raises 'r) -> A with 'e raises 'r
```

Runs `body` in a fresh region, discharging its `scope` requirement.

Row subtraction made concrete: `scope` is present in the body's requirement
row and absent from the result's. The region is an ordinary binding of this
function, so it ends when this function does — including when `body` raises
and the error passes straight through.

**Pass a named function, not a lambda**, for the reason on `nursery`.

### acquire

```khora
export fn acquire<A, 'e>(value: A, release: (A) ->()) -> A with { 'e | scope: Scope }
```

Acquires a value and registers its release in one step.

The generic half of `Scope`, kept out of the effect so the operation can
stay a plain closure. `release` is called with `value` when the region ends.

### attempt

```khora
export fn attempt<A, E, 'e>(body: () -> A with 'e raises E) -> Result<A, E> with 'e
```

Runs `body` and makes its failure a value.

The error channel and `Result` are the same thing said two ways — a tagged
return already *is* "an error or a value" — and this is where a caller
chooses which way to read it. The row of `body` is discharged, so what
comes back cannot fail again.

This is also what makes retrying possible: a policy that runs a computation
a second time has to be able to see that the first time did not work,
without knowing what it was doing.

### retry

```khora
export fn retry<A, E, 'e>(schedule: Schedule, body: () -> A with 'e raises E) -> A with 'e raises E
```

Runs `body` until it succeeds or the schedule runs out.

The last failure is the one that comes back, because it is the one that
stopped the retrying — an earlier error is a thing that was already
recovered from, and reporting it would say the wrong thing about what
happened.

### repeat

```khora
export fn repeat<A, E, 'e>(schedule: Schedule, body: () -> A with 'e raises E) -> Int with 'e
```

Runs `body` until it fails, or the schedule runs out. The count of runs
that succeeded comes back.
